analysis.summary:
This 32-year-old male presents with a one-year history of recurrent, inflammatory, itching skin lesions distributed across face, trunk, and limbs, accompanied by significant emotional distress and anxiety. The combination of physical symptoms with psychological stress indicates a stress-driven inflammatory skin condition rooted in deep constitutional imbalance rather than simple surface pathology.

Visual examination reveals a red tongue with teeth marks—a critical finding indicating Spleen Qi deficiency (the Spleen cannot transform and transport body fluids properly, causing the tongue to swell with retained fluid and show tooth impressions) combined with interior heat (red color). This single sign tells us the foundation is weak: the Spleen, responsible for healthy skin nutrition and fluid metabolism, is unable to function properly. Emotionally, the patient's description of feeling inferior and low due to visible symptoms, combined with heavy stress, points clearly to Liver Qi stagnation—the emotional stress and sense of social distress have disrupted Liver function.

The patient's symptom pattern—crimson plaques, dry itchy scaling, and importantly, itching that moves around the body—reflects Wind-Damp-Heat pathology at the skin surface. The migrating nature of the itch is characteristic of Wind in traditional medicine. The redness and heat point to Heat. However, the dry desquamation (flaking) indicates that Yin fluids are being consumed; this is not simple Damp but Damp complicated by Yin deficiency. The paradoxical temperature distribution (cool limbs and abdomen, hot upper body) reveals the deeper picture: the stress has depleted both Yin and Yang over time, and the Yin deficiency allows Yang Qi to float upward unchecked, generating heat in the upper body while the lower warmer becomes cold from Yang weakness.

The pathomechanism is a cascade: stress disrupts Liver Qi → Spleen loses the support it needs from Liver Qi → Spleen becomes weak and cannot transform Damp → Damp accumulates and combines with Heat (from inflammatory response and Liver dysfunction) → Wind-Damp-Heat erupts at the skin surface → visible condition causes emotional distress → stress worsens, perpetuating the cycle. Breaking this cycle requires addressing both the surface manifestation (Wind-Damp-Heat) and the root cause (Liver-Spleen dysfunction from stress), plus restoring the depleted Yin and Yang reserves.

This is precisely the type of condition where Traditional Chinese Medicine treatment excels: a stress-driven inflammatory disease with emotional and constitutional components. The prognosis is good if the patient commits to both herbal treatment (to move Liver Qi and restore Spleen function) and lifestyle/emotional management (to prevent stress from re-causing the problem). Skin improvement may take 8-12 weeks, but emotional and stress-response improvements typically manifest within 2-3 weeks, creating positive momentum for healing.

key_findings.from_inquiry: One-year progressive course of inflammatory skin lesions with emotional impact and clear stress causation; migrating/moving quality of itching suggesting Wind element; patient describing lower body and limbs as cool while upper body runs hot—this temperature inversion is key to understanding the constitutional deficiency; heavy psychological stress explicitly mentioned; anxiety as primary emotional manifestation; patient's sense of inferiority and low mood from visible condition creating emotional feedback loop.
key_findings.from_visual: Red tongue with teeth marks is the critical diagnostic finding—indicates Spleen Qi deficiency (cannot transform fluids, causing swelling and tooth indentations) combined with interior heat (red color). This explains both the Damp accumulation and the inflammatory response. No other visual findings recorded, but the teeth-marked red tongue is sufficient for pattern identification.
key_findings.from_pulse: Exact pulse qualities not captured in examination record; however, given the pattern of Spleen Qi deficiency with heat, expected pulse would be thin or moderate-force with accelerated rate, or possibly wiry (indicating Liver involvement from stress). Detailed pulse examination should be obtained at next visit to confirm and guide treatment modification.
key_findings.from_other: The combination of visible inflammatory skin lesions, emotional distress, stress causation, and constitutional coolness in lower body with heat in upper body creates a coherent picture that all points to the same underlying pattern. Each symptom element supports and reinforces the diagnosis of Damp-Heat with underlying Qi-Yin deficiency driven by Liver stress pathology.

analysis.pattern_rationale: The diagnosis of Wind-Damp-Heat with underlying Qi and Yin Deficiency is supported by multiple layers of evidence: (1) Direct skin manifestation: crimson inflammatory plaques with dry itching that moves around the body—this is the textbook presentation of Wind (moving quality), Damp (the lesion substance), and Heat (red color, inflammation); (2) Constitutional foundation: teeth-marked red tongue specifically indicates Spleen Qi deficiency unable to manage fluids properly combined with heat; (3) Temperature paradox: cool lower body/limbs with hot upper body indicates Yin deficiency (cannot anchor Yang) combined with underlying Yang deficiency in lower warmer—this is seen in chronic stress depletion; (4) Emotional component: anxiety, inferiority, explicit psychological stress clearly point to Liver Qi stagnation (Liver governs emotional smoothness); (5) Chronic course: one-year duration rules out acute pathogenic invasion and indicates constitutional derangement; (6) Feedback pattern: visible condition causing emotional distress which worsens stress which worsens skin—classic psychosomatic loop indicating Liver-Heart involvement. The secondary patterns of Liver Qi Stagnation and Heart Spirit Disturbance are not separate diagnoses but manifestations of the same underlying stress-driven disease process affecting multiple organ systems simultaneously.

treatment.therapeutic_principle: Move Liver Qi and resolve stagnation to address the root cause (stress); tonify Spleen Qi to restore proper fluid transformation and digestive function; clear Wind-Damp-Heat from the skin surface to resolve the acute manifestation; nourish Yin to restore constitutional reserves depleted by stress and heat; calm Heart spirit to interrupt the emotional feedback loop; reestablish harmony between upper and lower body temperatures through constitutional restoration.
treatment.treatment_method: Primary treatment via herbal medicine (Liver-Qi-moving formula with stress-relief and Spleen-tonifying properties); adjunctive acupressure on key Liver, Spleen, and Heart points for daily self-care; comprehensive lifestyle and dietary modification to prevent stress-related relapse and support healing; emotional/psychological support and stress-reduction practices to address the root cause; consistent sleep and hydration to restore depleted Yin; avoidance of inflammatory dietary triggers.

beneficial: Mung beans - Cool the heat of the inflammatory skin condition, support Spleen in transforming excess dampness, and provide easily-digestible plant protein; consume as soup or porridge 2-3 times weekly

Winter melon (Chinese white gourd) - Strongly drains pathogenic dampness, cools heat without damaging digestive function, provides gentle mineral support; excellent for this pattern, use fresh in soups

Job's tears grain (Coix grain) - Transforms and eliminates dampness while tonifying the weak Spleen; gentle and nourishing; particularly suited to this condition of Spleen Qi deficiency with Damp accumulation; consume 2-3 times weekly

Red dates (Jujubes) - Tonify Spleen Qi (addressing the weak foundation), nourish Heart blood (helping calm anxiety and emotional distress), and provide warmth to lower warmer without creating excess heat; consume 2-3 in daily cooking or tea

Goji berries (Lycium berries / Wolfberries) - Nourish Liver blood and Kidney Yin, directly addressing the depleted reserves from stress and heat; especially important for the dry skin manifestation; consume 1 small handful daily in tea or porridge
recipes: Mung Bean and Winter Melon Cooling Soup: Combine 200 grams dried mung beans (soaked 1 hour), 400 grams fresh winter melon (cut into chunks), 3-4 slices fresh ginger, 3 red dates (pitted). Boil mung beans for 20 minutes until partially soft, add winter melon and ginger, simmer 30 minutes, add red dates in final 10 minutes. Serve warm or room temperature. Consume 1 bowl 3 times weekly. This soup directly addresses the Damp-Heat by cooling and draining, while red dates tonify the weak Spleen foundation.

Job's Tears and Red Date Nourishing Congee (Rice Porridge): Combine 50 grams Job's tears grain (soaked 1 hour), 50 grams white rice, 3-4 red dates (pitted), 6-8 cups water. Small slice of fresh ginger may be added. Bring to boil, then simmer on low heat for 45-60 minutes until very thick and creamy, stirring occasionally. Ginger can be removed before eating. Consume warm as breakfast or light dinner, 4-5 times weekly. This porridge transforms dampness (Job's tears), tonifies Spleen and Qi (rice and red dates), and the congee form is easiest for weak digestive function to process. The warming preparation benefits the depleted lower warmer.

foods_to_avoid: Spicy foods (chili pepper, black pepper, garlic, ginger in excess) - Directly aggravate the Heat component of Wind-Damp-Heat; increase inflammatory response and further deplete body fluids; stimulate skin lesions to flare

Alcohol and fermented foods (alcohol, vinegar, soy sauce in excess, aged cheeses) - Alcohol generates internal heat and impairs Spleen function; fermented foods increase Damp accumulation; alcohol also disrupts Liver Qi movement and prevents healing

Fried and high-fat foods (deep-fried items, fatty meats, oily snacks) - Create excess Damp and Heat through their Heavy, Greasy nature; overwhelm weak Spleen function; prevent proper absorption of nutrients needed for skin healing

Sugar and refined carbohydrates (sweets, white bread, pastries, sugary drinks) - Damage Spleen function and promote Damp accumulation; inflammatory in nature; create energy crashes that worsen stress and emotional symptoms

Dairy products and milk (especially cooling types like yogurt or ice cream) - Can increase Damp accumulation in already-weak Spleen; cold temperature (in ice cream) directly damages Spleen Yang function
Shellfish with high iodine content (seaweed, shrimp in large quantities) - High iodine can trigger or worsen inflammatory skin reactions in sensitive individuals
lifestyle: Establish consistent sleep schedule supporting Yin restoration: Maintain sleep time of 10 PM to 6 AM with minimum 8 hours nightly. This is crucial because Yin (body fluids, essence, deep nourishment) is restored during sleep, and this patient has depleted Yin from stress and heat. Avoid late-night work or phone use which prevents deep sleep. Poor sleep directly worsens both skin condition and anxiety. Consider one 20-minute afternoon rest (1-2 PM) if schedule allows.

Maintain cool, dry physical environment: Keep living and sleeping spaces cool (68-72 Fahrenheit / 20-22 Celsius), well-ventilated, and dry. Avoid humid environments which exacerbate Damp pathology. Air conditioning during humid weather is beneficial. Change damp clothing immediately. Cool showers (not cold, but cool) are preferable to hot baths. Avoid saunas and steam rooms. This directly addresses the pathogenic Damp-Heat by preventing environmental perpetuation.

Daily stress reduction and gentle movement practice: Engage 20-30 minutes daily of Tai Chi, gentle Yoga (especially Yin Yoga holding poses 3-5 minutes), or quiet walking in nature. These practices move Liver Qi gently without generating heat, calm the Heart spirit, and reduce anxiety. Avoid intense exercise (running, weight lifting, hot yoga) that generates internal heat and further depletes Yin. This directly addresses the root cause (Liver stress) rather than just surface symptoms.

Mindfulness and emotional processing: Practice 10-15 minutes daily of meditation, deep breathing, or journaling to process emotions and prevent Liver Qi stagnation from re-accumulating. When stress arises, pause and take 3-5 deep breaths. Address underlying stressors in life if possible—whether work pressure, relationship issues, or perfectionism—through counseling or life changes. The skin condition is partly a message from the body that emotional stress must be addressed. acceptance and self-compassion toward the skin condition during healing prevents negative emotions from worsening the pattern.

Eat meals in calm, regular schedule: Consume meals at consistent times (breakfast 7-8 AM, lunch 12-1 PM, dinner 5-6 PM) in a calm, unhurried environment. Avoid eating while working, stressed, or angry, as emotional disruption impairs Spleen digestion. Eat until 70% full, not to excess. The weak Spleen cannot process large meals or food consumed in haste. This simple practice substantially improves digestive function and prevents Damp accumulation.
acupoints: Large Intestine 11 (Pool at the Bend) - Located at the lateral end of the elbow crease when the arm is flexed to 90 degrees. Using thumb or knuckle, apply firm circular pressure for 1-2 minutes, massaging in small circles around the point. This point clears heat and resolves inflammatory skin lesions; particularly important for this Heat-manifesting pattern.

Stomach 36 (Leg Three Miles) - Located 3 hand-widths below the lower edge of the kneecap (below point Stomach 35), one finger-width lateral to the anterior tibial crest (the bone ridge you feel on the front of the lower leg). Apply firm thumb pressure with gentle circular massage for 2-3 minutes daily. This is the master point for tonifying Qi and strengthening Spleen function—critical for addressing the weak foundation (teeth-marked tongue). Regular stimulation of this point strengthens overall constitution and prevents relapse.

Liver 3 (Great Rushing) - Located in the webbing between the first and second toe, in the depression proximal to where the metatarsal bones meet. Apply gentle thumb pressure, working both feet, for 1-2 minutes. This point moves Liver Qi stagnation, reduces stress, and helps break the emotional feedback loop perpetuating the skin condition. Particularly important given the stress-driven nature of this case.

Heart 7 (Spirit Gate) - Located on the wrist crease on the pinky side (ulnar border), in the depression at the wrist line. Apply gentle thumb pressure and small circular motions for 1-2 minutes, preferably in evening or before bed. This point calms Heart spirit, reduces anxiety and insomnia, and interrupts the emotional component of the disease. Important for breaking the psychological stress cycle.

Spleen 9 (Yin Mound Spring) - Located on the inner (medial) surface of the lower leg, in the depression below and slightly behind the bony bump on the inner knee (medial tibial condyle). Apply firm thumb pressure with circular massage for 1-2 minutes daily. This point transforms dampness and strengthens Spleen function—directly targets the Damp pathology component. Essential for this pattern.
exercise: Tai Chi or gentle flowing movement - 20-30 minutes, 4-5 times weekly. Tai Chi is ideal because it moves Liver Qi smoothly without generating internal heat, strengthens the body without exhaustion, and has well-documented benefits for stress and anxiety. Alternatively, gentle flowing yoga or qigong movements. Avoid fast-paced or vigorous exercise which depletes Yin and worsens heat.

Walking in nature - 30 minutes daily at comfortable, conversational pace. Can be informal (walking to work, around neighborhood) or structured (nature trails, park walking). This provides gentle exercise, stress relief through nature exposure, and regular Qi movement without heat generation. Walking is universally appropriate for this pattern.
recommendations.emotional_care: The emotional component is not secondary but central to this condition. Because Liver Qi stagnation from stress is driving much of the pathology, emotional wellbeing is as important as herbal medicine and diet. Establish daily practices: meditation or mindfulness (10-15 minutes), journaling about emotions and stressors, time in nature, engagement in activities that bring joy and meaning, cultivation of social connection and support, and where possible, addressing the underlying life stressors (job pressure, relationship issues, perfectionism, life dissatisfaction). Consider counseling or therapy if stress is from major life difficulties. Practice self-compassion and acceptance toward the skin condition during healing—harsh judgment of the visible symptoms creates negative emotion that worsens Liver Qi stagnation and perpetuates the skin condition. Many patients find that as they reduce stress and improve emotional state, skin lesions improve dramatically even before herbal medicine takes full effect. The body-mind connection is real in this condition.

warning_signs: Rapid spread of lesions beyond previous boundaries despite treatment—may indicate need for conventional dermatological evaluation or formula adjustment

Signs of infection: increasing warmth, redness intensifying, purulent (pus-like) drainage, swelling of surrounding tissue, tender lymph nodes in nearby areas—these require immediate conventional medical evaluation
Fever accompanying skin symptoms—suggests possible secondary infection requiring antibiotics
Severe systemic symptoms: unexplained weight loss, extreme fatigue, night sweats beyond normal stress-related sweating, fever—may indicate underlying disease requiring conventional workup
Severe allergic reaction signs: swelling of face, lips, tongue, or throat; difficulty breathing; urinary retention or incontinence; severe dizziness—seek emergency care immediately
Lesions showing no improvement after 12 weeks of consistent herbal treatment and lifestyle modifications—may require alternative approach or evaluation for other diagnoses
New, unexpected symptoms appearing during treatment—report to TCM practitioner for assessment
contraindications: Scratching the lesions—this is the most damaging habit; scratching perpetuates inflammation, can cause secondary infection, and prolongs the healing cycle. Keep fingernails short and clean; use distraction techniques or cold compress instead of scratching when itching is intense.

Exposure to heat and deliberate overheating—heat aggravates the Heat component of the pattern; avoid hot baths, saunas, steam rooms, intense sun exposure, and heavy exercise that causes profuse sweating
Consumption of spicy foods, alcohol, and inflammatory foods listed above—these directly exacerbate Wind-Damp-Heat and worsen both skin and emotional symptoms
Prolonged emotional stress or avoidance of stress-management practices—since stress is driving the root cause, avoiding emotional work prevents healing despite herbal medicine

Chronic topical steroid cream application—while short-term steroids (1-2 weeks) may be appropriate for severe flares under medical supervision, long-term steroid use thins skin and creates dependency; avoid without medical guidance

Discontinuing herbal medicine prematurely—skin conditions typically require minimum 8 weeks of consistent treatment; stopping early often leads to relapse when Qi stagnation re-accumulates from stress
precautions.special_notes: Before commencing this TCM treatment protocol, confirm with a conventional dermatologist that the presentation is not fungal infection (which requires antifungal treatment), bacterial infection, or contagious condition. If dermatological diagnosis has been made (psoriasis, atopic eczema, lichen planus, contact dermatitis), TCM can be used as adjunctive treatment alongside conventional care. This particular presentation—chronic, non-infectious, exacerbated by stress, associated with anxiety—is highly amenable to TCM treatment because the root is constitutional and emotional rather than acute pathogenic. The strong psychosomatic component (stress triggers flares, visible condition causes emotional distress) makes simultaneous attention to emotional wellbeing crucial for success. Herbal medicine alone without lifestyle and stress management will show limited results. Conversely, patients who commit fully to both herbal treatment and lifestyle change often see dramatic improvement. The condition is not dangerous to life but can significantly impact quality of life; treatment is justified both medically and for quality-of-life reasons. This is one of the conditions where TCM has strong evidence-based benefits in clinical practice.

follow_up.timeline: Reassess progress at 4 weeks of starting herbal medicine and lifestyle modifications. At 4-week mark, patient should report to TCM practitioner for evaluation of initial response and potential formula adjustment if needed. Continue reassessment every 2-4 weeks until clear improvement trend is established. Total minimum treatment course is 8-12 weeks for this pattern; many patients require 12-16 weeks for complete lesion resolution.
follow_up.expected_improvement: Week 1-2: Reduced intensity of anxiety and stress response is often first sign (patients report feeling calmer, better emotional resilience); sleep may improve. Week 2-3: Itching may become less constant; note whether itching is less intense or less frequent. Week 4: Notable reduction in itching; skin may appear slightly less red or inflamed. Week 4-6: Reduction in lesion count or size; scaling may become less prominent; patient reports improved quality of life. Week 6-12: Progressive resolution of lesions; improvement in skin appearance; anxiety and emotional symptoms continue improving; energy and overall sense of wellbeing improve. Timeline varies by individual; some improve faster, some slower. Slower responders should not lose hope—skin conditions from deep constitutional imbalance often take 12-16 weeks for full resolution but improvement should be evident by 4-6 weeks if treatment is correct.
follow_up.next_steps: At 4-week assessment: (1) If good improvement seen—continue same formula, maintain lifestyle changes, plan reassessment in 4 weeks; (2) If minimal improvement—TCM practitioner should modify formula approach, possibly adding more heat-clearing herbs or adjusting dosage, and explore whether patient is consistently following lifestyle recommendations and whether stress is still driving the condition; (3) If excellent improvement—may begin slowly extending herbal dosing interval (e.g., once daily instead of twice daily) while continuing to monitor, planning eventual tapering; (4) At 8-week point—if significant improvement, continue herbal support but plan to taper over 2-4 weeks, then transition to maintenance approach of continued lifestyle management; (5) Following resolution of skin lesions—maintain ongoing stress management, sleep habits, dietary modifications, and acupoint self-massage indefinitely, as cessation of these will likely allow stress-related relapse. Consider follow-up herbal medicine courses at seasonal transitions (spring, autumn) or during high-stress periods as preventive care.
